quote: There is a story that one of the first men to realize that stars were burning by fusion—plausible attributions I’ve seen are to Fritz Houtermans and Hans Bethe—was walking out with his girlfriend of a night
content: The story is Houtermans’s, told about a walk with Charlotte Riefenstahl (whom he later married) in 1929, and its source is Robert Jungk’s Brighter than a Thousand Suns (1956), a book whose reliability on the physicists it profiles is poor enough that its account of Heisenberg and the German bomb was repudiated by Heisenberg’s own colleagues. What Houtermans and Atkinson showed in 1929 was that Gamow’s quantum tunnelling made nuclear reactions possible at stellar temperatures; that stars burn by subatomic energy had been proposed by Eddington in 1920, who wrote that “the hydrogen which is transformed into helium” was the likely source, and the specific proton–proton and CNO cycles were Bethe’s, a decade later. So “the only man in the world who knows why they shine” was, at best, the only man who knew one step of it, and his priority was shared with a co-author. The essay uses the anecdote to illustrate an emotion, and the emotion is real; but the essay’s program is to bind feeling to fact, and the fact here is that the man with the girlfriend did not know why the stars shine, and said so in a book that got other things wrong.

quote: The studies showing that subjecting fraternity pledges to a harsher initiation, causes them to be more convinced of the value of the fraternity—identical wine in higher-priced bottles being rated as tasting better—that sort of thing.
content: No fraternity study exists in the form described. The effort-justification experiment is Aronson & Mills (1959), in which women who read embarrassing sexual material aloud as a “screening test” rated a dull discussion group about sex more favourably than those who read mild material; sixty-three participants, a one-item outcome, a modest effect. Gerard & Mathewson (1966) replicated it with electric shock in place of embarrassment. The general finding is real but small and its boundary conditions are poorly mapped; it is one of the dissonance paradigms that the replication-era reviews rate as “probably real, effect size uncertain.” The wine finding is Plassmann et al. (2008), twenty participants in a scanner, and it has replicated (Schmidt et al. (2017)), so that part stands. The essay’s use is fair as far as it goes; the annotation is here because the “fraternity pledges” version is the textbook garbling of a study that was about something else, and because the same book’s Initiation Ceremony, four essays later, designs an initiation ritual in earnest on the strength of the effect the essay here calls the less charitable reading.

quote: And really the situation is even worse than this, because in the Standard Model of physics (discovered by bastards who spoiled the puzzle for everyone else) the universe is spatially infinite, inflationarily branching, and branching via decoherence, which is at least three different ways that Reality is exponentially or infinitely large.
content: None of the three is in the Standard Model, which is the quantum field theory of the strong and electroweak interactions and says nothing about cosmology. Spatial infinity is an inference from measured flatness, and flatness is measured to a tolerance, not established; the Planck 2018 data are consistent with a flat universe and were read by one group as preferring a closed one (Di Valentino, Melchiorri & Silk (2020)), a reading others dispute, which is where “infinite” actually stands. Eternal inflation is a speculative extension of inflation whose predictions are notoriously hard to extract (the measure problem), and one of inflation’s founders has argued against it in print (Steinhardt (2011)). Branching via decoherence is the Everett interpretation, argued for later in this book and, as Opus’s annotation on Many Worlds records, a minority view among physicists. The essay needs Reality to be enormous so that the joy of discovery can be shared out; it obtains the enormousness by attributing three contested claims to the best-confirmed theory in physics.

quote: It is attested by numerous sources that this experience, being the first person to solve a major mystery, is a tremendous high. It’s probably the closest experience you can get to taking drugs, without taking drugs—though I wouldn’t know.
content: The physiology supports the essay, and it supports the essay’s preferred conclusion rather than the “exclusivity clause” it worries about. Insight solutions to puzzles, compared with the same problems solved analytically, are accompanied by activation in the nucleus accumbens and ventral striatum, the reward circuitry that drugs of abuse act on (Tik et al. (2018)), and the subjective “Aha!” reliably carries positive affect and a burst of confidence. Every participant in those studies was solving a problem that the experimenters, and thousands of previous participants, had already solved. The high does not require being first; it requires having been stuck. That is the essay’s “most charitable interpretation,” and it is the one the evidence favours, so the essay’s worry that the joy of discovery might be “one-shot per civilization” can be retired on empirical grounds rather than by the multiverse argument the essay reaches for instead.
